items.label: section_header
items.text: HOW TO WORK OUT THE ARRANGEMENT OF ELECTRONS IN ANATOM

items.label: section_header
items.text: DRAWING DIAGRAMS OF ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATIONS DRAWING DIAGRAMS OF ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATIONS

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: The arrangement of electrons in an atom is called its electronic configuration.

items.label: text
items.text: We will use chlorine as an example.

items.label: text
items.text: Look up the atomic number in the Periodic Table. (Make sure that you don't use the wrong number if you have a choice. The atomic number will always be the smaller one.)

items.label: text
items.text: The Periodic Table tells you that chlorine's atomic number is 17.

items.label: text
items.text: This tells you the number of protons. The number of electrons is equal to the number of protons.

items.label: text
items.text: There are 17 protons and so 17 electrons in a neutral chlorine atom.

items.label: text
items.text: Arrange the electrons in shells (energy levels), always completing an inner shell (lower energy level) before you go to an outer one. Remember that the first sh  n  t s   n   (   ake up to 8, and the third one also takes up to 8.

items.label: text
items.text: For chlorine the electrons will be arranged as follows: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second shell and 7 in the third shell. This is written as 2, 8, 7. When you have finished, always check to make sure that the electrons add up to the right number, in this case 17.

items.label: text
items.text: When we draw a diagram of an atom we usually draw circles to represent the shells (energy levels); dots or crosses are then drawn on the circles to represent the electrons. You can choose to draw dots or crosses.

items.label: text
items.text: Hydrogen has 1 electron and helium has 2 in the first shell (lowest energy level).

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 4.4 Electronic arrangements of hydrogen and helium

items.label: text
items.text: Drawing circles like this does not imply that the electrons are orbiting the nucleus along the circles.

items.label: text
items.text: The circles represent energy levels. The further away the level is from the nucleus, the higher its energy. It is impossible to work out exactly how an electron is moving in that

items.label: text
items.text: energy level.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT HINT

items.label: text
items.text: The terms 'shell' and 'energy level' are used quite interchangeably by chemists. To make things easier, we will just use one term, shell, from now on. If, however, you prefer the term energy level, that is absolutely fine and both terms will be accepted in the examination.
